      Assembly

Experimental Engineering (E80)

AUV Ocean Floor SONAR Mapping



  
    
  
  
    
      Overview:
      Designed and built an AUV to topographically map the floor of Dana Point Harbor using SONAR time-of-flight measurements. Personally designed analog circuits for temperature, pressure, and SONAR signal processing — all from scratch. Featured a Teensy 4.0, Adafruit GPS, and a custom motor driver motherboard.
    
    Skills:Arduino, MATLAB, SONAR, Embedded Systems, PCB Assembly, Op-Amp Circuit Design, Sensor Calibration
    
      
        Show More
      
      
        See Report Page
      
    
  



  
    
      Custom Sensor Circuits
      
      
        - Designed a thermistor interface circuit with a unity gain buffer and non-inverting offset amplifier to expand the output voltage range for better Teensy resolution.
        - Built a pressure sensor circuit with the same offset amplifier approach to enable precise P-control during dives.
        - For SONAR, designed both a TX chain (555 timer + LM384 audio amplifier driving a waterproof exciter at 3kHz) and a full RX chain with 10,000x gain across four op-amp stages, a Sallen-Key bandpass filter, and a max detector circuit.
      
    
    
      Deployment at Dana Point
      
      
        - Deployed the AUV at Dana Point Harbor, following alongside in kayaks to monitor and recover it.
        - GPS module handled surface navigation while the pressure sensor controlled dive depth autonomously via P-control.
        - All sensor data was logged to an onboard SD card and post-processed in MATLAB to generate the topography map.
      
    
    
      Results & Presentation
      
      
        - Successfully mapped the ocean floor depth along the AUV's path, with results consistent with nautical chart ground truth data for Dana Point Harbor.
        - Also measured water temperature at depth and confirmed a temperature decrease with depth during dives.
        - Presented findings at the end-of-semester showcase — our team took first place!

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
Introduction
In this lab, a quadrature encoder on a 25GA-370 brushed DC motor was used to measure motor speed and direction with the STM32L432KC MCU. GPIO external interrupts (EXTI) on both edges of both encoder channels detect every encoder pulse, and the speed in rev/s and direction are printed at a 2 Hz update rate.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

MCU
The two encoder channels are connected to PA6 and PA8, which are 5V-tolerant (FT) pins on the STM32L432KC per the datasheet’s pin table, so no level-shifting circuit is needed. Both pins are configured as inputs with the internal pull-ups enabled.
PA6 and PA8 share the EXTI9_5_IRQHandler interrupt, and both are set to trigger on the rising and falling edge. Every edge of both channels therefore generates an interrupt, giving the highest possible resolution. The ISR is kept short: it clears the pending bit, reads both channels, and adds or subtracts one from enc_count depending on direction (on an A edge, A != B is forward; on a B edge, A == B is forward).
The main loop uses TIM2 to wait out a 500 ms sampling window. It then briefly disables interrupts to copy and reset enc_count, converts the count to rev/s, and prints the speed and direction (forward, reverse, or stopped) based on the sign of the count. If the motor is not spinning, no interrupts occur and the speed is reported as zero.


Calculations
TIM2 runs from the default 4 MHz clock with PSC = 3999, giving a 1 ms tick. With ARR = 500, each sampling window lasts:
\[
T_{\text{window}} = \frac{500}{1\,\text{kHz}} = 0.5\,\text{s} \quad \Rightarrow \quad f_{\text{update}} = 2\,\text{Hz} \geq 1\,\text{Hz}
\]
The encoder outputs 408 pulses per output shaft revolution on each channel. Since both edges of both channels are counted, the counts per revolution is:
\[
\text{CPR} = 408 \times 4 = 1632\,\text{counts/rev}
\]
The speed is the number of counts in the window divided by the counts per revolution and the window length:
\[
\text{rev/s} = \frac{\text{counts}}{\text{CPR} \times T_{\text{window}}} = \frac{\text{counts}}{1632 \times 0.5\,\text{s}}
\]
A single count corresponds to \(1/1632 = 0.22^\circ\) of shaft rotation, so the smallest non-zero speed the system can measure (one count per window) is:
\[
\text{Resolution} = \frac{1}{1632 \times 0.5\,\text{s}} \approx 0.0012\,\text{rev/s}
\]

Lab 3: Keypad Input with Finite State Machines
text: In this lab, a debounced, single-registration keypad reader was implemented on the UPduino v3.1 FPGA, reusing the 4x4 matrix keypad, 2N3904/2N3906 transistor drivers, and dual seven-segment display wired for Lab 2. Rather than continuously reading the scanned keypad columns onto LEDs, this lab synchronizes the asynchronous keypad inputs, debounces the mechanical switch bounce inherent to the keypad, and uses a finite state machine to register each keypress exactly once regardless of how long the key is held. The dual seven-segment display, reused unchanged from Lab 2, shows the last two hexadecimal digits pressed.

FSM Communication
The design is made up of five communicating FSMs:

Keypad FSM (keypadFSM): the main controller, which decides when to scan, debounce, and register a key.
Scanning sequence (scanning): cycles through the keypad rows. The keypad FSM stops it on the active row with scanEn when a key is pressed.
Debounce timer (debounceTimer): counts while the keypad FSM is in DEBOUNCE, and sends dbDone when the time is up.
Digit register (digitRegister): stores the last two keys pressed, and shifts in a new digit when the keypad FSM pulses newKey.
Display multiplexing: alternates between the two digits stored in the digit register on the dual seven-segment display.



Switch Debouncing Strategy
When a key is pressed, the keypad FSM waits for the duration of a typical button bounce (20 ms, or 480,000 clock cycles at 24 MHz). Once that time has passed, the debounce timer sends dbDone to tell the FSM to continue and register the key.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Input with Finite State Machines
text:
Conclusion
This lab built on the display and keypad hardware from Lab 2 by adding synchronization, debouncing, and a finite state machine to turn raw, bouncy switch contacts into a single clean event per keypress. Reusing the Lab 2 scanning, decoder, and multiplexing logic kept the new HDL focused on the FSM and debounce logic, and demonstrated how a fully synchronous design with strobed enables avoids the metastability and glitching problems that come with asynchronous keypad inputs.






NoteHours Spent on Lab



This lab took 23 hours.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text: In this lab, a time-multiplexed dual 7-segment display and a keypad scanning circuit were implemented using the UPduino v3.1 FPGA. Two independent 4-bit hexadecimal values are provided via DIP switches: one from the on-board switch and one from a breadboard DIP switch. These two values are displayed simultaneously on a dual 7-segment display by rapidly alternating between the two digits, so that a single shared sevenSegment decoder module and a single set of cathode pins drive both digits. A 2N3906 PNP transistor circuit sources the large anode current required by each digit. A scanning circuit drives the four rows of a matrix keypad through 2N3904 NPN transistors wired as open-collector outputs, and the four keypad columns are read back into the FPGA and driven out onto LEDs, so that pressing a key lights the LED for its column.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Introduction
In this lab, a hardware timer of the STM32L432KC MCU was used to drive an 8-ohm speaker to play music. The timer was used to toggle a GPIO pin at a specified frequency, generating a square wave for each musical note, and also to produce millisecond delays for rests. The system was tested by playing Fur Elise, and as an optional piece, Fallen Down was also implemented.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

Lab Overview
A single timer, TIM2, was used for both frequency generation and duration control. For each note, ARR is reloaded to set the correct half-period, and the GPIO pin is flipped on every update event, producing a square wave. The note’s duration is set by how many times the pin is toggled. For rests, the GPIO pin is held low and ARR is set for a 1 ms tick, looping for the required number of milliseconds. After every note the pin is forced low so the speaker never sits at a DC level during a rest.
All peripheral registers of RCC, GPIO, and TIM2 were defined by hand as structs mapped to base addresses and offsets from the STM32L432KC Reference Manual. No CMSIS headers were used!


Clock and Timer Configuration
The MCU runs on its default 4 MHz MSI clock. The AHB and APB1 prescalers are both left at 1, so TIM2, which sits on the APB1 bus, receives a 4 MHz clock. Its clock is turned on with the TIM2EN bit in RCC->APB1ENR1. The prescaler (PSC) is set to 3, dividing the 4 MHz clock by 4 to produce a 1 MHz timer clock (1 µs per tick):
\[
f_{\text{timer}} = \frac{4\,\text{MHz}}{PSC + 1} = \frac{4\,\text{MHz}}{4} = 1\,\text{MHz}
\]


Frequency Generation
The counter counts from 0 to ARR, so an update event occurs every ARR + 1 ticks. The GPIO pin toggles on each update event, so one update period is half of the square wave’s period. The output frequency is therefore:
\[
f_{\text{out}} = \frac{f_{\text{timer}}}{2\,(\text{ARR}+1)}
= \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2\,(\text{ARR}+1)}
\]
Solving for ARR, and noting that the C code uses integer division (which rounds down):
\[
\text{ARR} = \left\lfloor\frac{f_{\text{timer}}}{2f}\right\rfloor - 1 = \left\lfloor\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2f}\right\rfloor - 1
\]


Duration Control (Notes)
A note of duration \(d\) milliseconds needs \(2f\) toggles per second, so the code toggles the pin
\[
N = \left\lfloor \frac{2 f d}{1000} \right\rfloor
\]
times. Each toggle takes one half-period, so the actual duration is
\[
d_{\text{actual}} = N \cdot (\text{ARR}+1)\ \mu\text{s}
\]


Duration Control (Rests)
For rests (freq == 0), the delay function sets ARR to produce a 1 ms tick:
\[
\text{ARR}_{\text{delay}} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{1{,}000} - 1 = 999
\]
The loop then counts \(d\) update events, so a rest of \(d\) ms is exact.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Calculations

Frequency Range
The possible frequency range follows from the smallest and largest usable ARR. Because TIM2 is a 32-bit timer, ARR_max = \(2^{32} - 1\) = 4,294,967,295. ARR_min is 1: the Reference Manual states that the counter is blocked while ARR is 0.
\[
f_{\text{min}} = \frac{f_{\text{timer}}}{2 \times (\text{ARR}_{\text{max}} + 1)} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times 2^{32}} \approx 0.000116\,\text{Hz}
\]
\[
f_{\text{max}} = \frac{f_{\text{timer}}}{2 \times (\text{ARR}_{\text{min}} + 1)} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times 2} = 250{,}000\,\text{Hz}
\]
These are the hardware limits. In practice, frequencies are stored as integers and 0 means a rest, so the lowest note that can be requested is 1 Hz. This comfortably covers the required 220–1000 Hz range.


Duration Range
Minimum: durations are integer milliseconds, so \[
d_{\text{min}} = 1\,\text{ms}
\]
Maximum (rests): the duration is passed as a signed 32-bit int, so \[
d_{\text{max,rest}} = 2^{31}-1 = 2{,}147{,}483{,}647\,\text{ms} = \frac{2{,}147{,}483{,}647}{86{,}400{,}000\,\text{ms/day}} \approx 24.8\,\text{days}
\]
Maximum (notes): 2 * freq * delay is computed as a signed 32-bit int and overflows past \(2^{31}-1\). At the highest note in Fur Elise (1319 Hz): \[
d_{\text{max,note}} = \left\lfloor \frac{2^{31}-1}{2 \times 1319} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{2{,}147{,}483{,}647}{2638} \right\rfloor = 814{,}057\,\text{ms} \approx 13.6\,\text{min}
\]


Frequency Accuracy (220 Hz and 1000 Hz)
220 Hz: \[
\text{ARR} = \left\lfloor\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times 220}\right\rfloor - 1 = \lfloor 2272.73 \rfloor - 1 = 2271
\] \[
f_{\text{actual}} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times (2271 + 1)} = 220.07\,\text{Hz}, \qquad \text{error} = \frac{220.07 - 220}{220} = 0.03\%
\]
1000 Hz: \[
\text{ARR} = \left\lfloor\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times 1000}\right\rfloor - 1 = 500 - 1 = 499
\] \[
f_{\text{actual}} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times (499 + 1)} = 1000.00\,\text{Hz}, \qquad \text{error} = 0.00\%
\]


Fur Elise Accuracy
The table below applies the formulas above to every distinct note in Fur Elise. Error is measured against the frequency stored in the notes array. For example, for E5 (659 Hz):
\[
\text{ARR} = \left\lfloor\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times 659}\right\rfloor - 1 = \lfloor 758.73 \rfloor - 1 = 757
\] \[
f_{\text{actual}} = \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{2 \times (757 + 1)} = 659.631\,\text{Hz}, \qquad \text{error} = \frac{659.631 - 659}{659} = 0.096\%
\]

NoteSource Code

PA1 was configured as a general-purpose output by enabling the GPIOA clock via RCC->AHB2ENR and setting its MODER field to 01. TIM2 was enabled via RCC->APB1ENR1. All registers were accessed through hand-written struct typedefs, meaning no CMSIS headers! Very bare-metal C code.

NoteExpand to see Schematic











Figure 1: Schematic of the Nucleo STM32L432KC MCU, LM386 amplifier, 10 kΩ potentiometer, and 8-ohm A0202C speaker.






The PA1 output was connected through a 10 kΩ potentiometer, wired as a voltage divider with its wiper feeding the non-inverting input of the LM386 amplifier, which provided adjustable volume. The LM386 was powered from the 5 V MCU supply, and its output drove the 8-ohm speaker.
No components on the development board were used in this lab. Every component shown in Figure 1 is off-board, on the breadboard.

Conclusion
The design successfully met all lab requirements. Fur Elise played at the correct tempo, with every pitch, including the 1319 Hz E6, within 1% error, as verified by the ARR calculations above. All rests were rendered as silence for the correct durations. The optional composition Fallen Down also played correctly! And the potentiometer varied the volume as intended.






NoteHours Spent on Lab



This lab took approximately 15 hours to complete. The most time-consuming parts were navigating the reference manual to find the correct register offsets, and understanding C code in a more thorough way.

text:
AI Prototype Summary
The purpose of the AI Prototype is to experiment with utilizing AI as a coding assistant, and analyze the quality, speed, and precision with which an LLM can generate code. The prompt for this week is shown below:






TipAI Prototype (Claude Sonnet)



Prompt: What timers should I use on the STM32L432KC to generate frequencies ranging from 220Hz to 1kHz? What’s the best choice of timer if I want to easily connect it to a GPIO pin? What formulae are relevant, and what registers need to be set to configure them properly?



Reflection:
This week is Claude Sonnet. Claude Sonnet claimed that the following timers would work for generating 220 Hz to 1 kHz frequencies: TIM1, TIM2, TIM15, and TIM16. This makes sense, as I had used TIM2. It chose TIM2 as the best option due to its resolution, number of channels, and ease of access.
It also gave the following formula:
\[
f_{output} = \frac{f_{TIMx\_CLK}}{(PSC + 1) \times (ARR + 1)}
\]
with an example for 440 Hz (A4) with PWM. This formula has no factor of 2 because in PWM mode the timer hardware produces one full output period per update, whereas my code toggles the pin in software on each update, so it needs two updates per period.
It also gave the maximum and minimum ARR as 4544 and 999 for a PSC of 79. These check out if the MCU is run at 80 MHz: \(80\,\text{MHz}/(79+1) = 1\,\text{MHz}\), so 220 Hz needs \(\text{ARR} = 10^6/220 - 1 \approx 4544\) and 1000 Hz needs \(\text{ARR} = 10^6/1000 - 1 = 999\). My design runs at the default 4 MHz, so I used PSC = 3 to get the same 1 MHz timer clock.
Claude Sonnet also provided the correct register configuration, and how to enable the clocks with RCC, and even configure the GPIO pin! Overall the LLM returned mostly correct information, but it gave more information than I asked for.

Submitted to IEEE
  Stress, Cognitive Load, and Specifications Grading in an Engineering Laboratory Course
  
    Cleo McHenry, Sara Morishige, Jasmine Sampat, Joaquin Gonzalez-Salgado, Leah Uriarte, Matthew Spencer
  
  IEEE Transactions on Education, 2025
  
    This paper presents a controlled two-year experiment at Harvey Mudd College studying how two evidence-based
    interventions — simplified lab manuals and specifications grading — affected student stress and cognitive load
    in a required sophomore engineering lab course (E80). Weekly validated surveys showed that stress was
    significantly reduced in six of seven labs, and cognitive load dropped significantly in three. Students in
    the treatment cohort also posted meaningfully higher scores on a summative technical memo, suggesting the
    interventions did not harm learning. I contributed as a co-author on the study design, data collection,
    and analysis.
  
  
    *Currently being published*
  




  Report
  Autonomous Surface & Dive Robot for Underwater Depth Mapping
  
    Joaquin Gonzalez-Salgado, Esteban Gonzalez, Ayla Greenstein, Kathy Guo
  
  E80: Experimental Engineering, Harvey Mudd College — Spring 2026
  
    This report documents the design, construction, and field deployment of an autonomous underwater vehicle
    (AUV) built to map the seafloor topography of Dana Point Harbor. The vehicle integrated a SONAR depth
    sensor (CME1538-100LB microphone + daex25W-8 speaker), an MPX5700ASX pressure sensor for dive depth,
    and a thermistor for temperature profiling across depth. The AUV featured four horizontal and two vertical
    thrusters, a low center of gravity for surface stability, and a winch-based recovery system. Deployment
    at Dana Point produced a topographic depth map of the harbor floor, with real-time data logging to an
    onboard SD card. Sensor drift from ocean currents affected positional accuracy, motivating future work
    on closed-loop horizontal control.
